First steps — why uniqueness needs an assumption

This example deliberately starts with a counterexample: existence does not imply uniqueness. In Use this history; find facts mode, the checker chooses truth values for chosen(red) and chosen(blue). SomeChoice requires at least one, but permits both; UniqueChoice requires exactly one. A model with both values chosen therefore satisfies the assumption and falsifies the property. No protocol events or intermediate time stages are needed: even the empty history has its end-of-time world.

To supply the missing guarantee, choose Edit Markdown, change the formula of SomeChoice to ∃=1 v. chosen(v), choose Update choices, and run again. With the starting selections, UniqueChoice then holds within the selected scope. A supplied-model check has a different task: it evaluates the explicit facts, treating absent facts as false.

Use Return to previous example and Continue to next example to browse the curated set. Loading another example clears the preceding results; it does not run the new example automatically.

Read the rules below, choose Continue to claims, review the selected properties and assumptions, then continue to the run settings and run the check. Use Edit Markdown to change a rule; Unicode and ASCII spellings have identical semantics. The supplied history JSON is at the end.

Assumptions and protocol rules

SomeChoice — other assumption

At least one domain value is chosen. Both values may still be chosen.

# Scenario: added for this experiment; not a paper axiom or correctness claim. Definition 3.3.3, p. 24.
axiom SomeChoice [other]:
  ∃ v. chosen(v)

Properties to check

These claims test the declared finite scenario. Their validity scope is shown on each property.

UniqueChoice — property

Exactly one domain value is chosen. The existential assumption above does not supply uniqueness.

# Scenario: added for this experiment; not a paper axiom or correctness claim. Definition 3.6.1, p. 31; Figure 5, p. 31.
property UniqueChoice [end]:
  ∃=1 v. chosen(v)

HBBSafe — completed broadcast

This is a completed one-participant run of HBBSafe, using the axioms and correctness statements from the draft of 18 November 2026. Choose Use this history; find facts first. The given positive facts pin liveness and safety; the retained axioms constrain the remaining predicate interpretation.

The final silent † tuple records knowledge of delivery. It is not an extra protocol event. Removing that observation can violate the Knowledge scheme, even though delivery itself has occurred.

The correctness formulas include their stated premises. A true implication may be vacuous. For a direct non-vacuity investigation, the API supplies the corresponding scenario formulas through correctnessProperties("HBBSafe"). In this completed singleton example all three scenarios occur.

Read the rules below, choose Continue to claims, review the selected properties and assumptions, then continue to the run settings and run the check. Use Edit Markdown to change a rule; Unicode and ASCII spellings have identical semantics. The supplied history JSON is at the end.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 43, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 42).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires both current safe(l) and knowledge of a quorum of prior matching echoes.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ (safe(l) ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a reporting quorum of matching source-learner votes.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. deliver(m,l,v) ⇒ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

Safe — other assumption

Safety is a biconditional: at most one proposal value is known, or every learner has a sequential witness in every relevant quorum intersection.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Safe [other]:
  ∀ l. safe(l) ⇔ ((∃⩽1 v. ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ∨ (∀ m. ♢[l,m] seq))

Echo! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a proposal, that participant must echo some value at an actual local tuple. The value is existentially chosen; end-of-time knowledge alone does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of echoes, that participant must vote at an actual local tuple. The rule does not impose a time order between those two tuples. Its separate ⇕ safe(l) guard requires safety at every actual local tuple; the required vote is for the same value.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ⇕ safe(l) ⇒ ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ↕ vote(l,v)

Deliver! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of votes, that participant must deliver at an actual local tuple. Merely learning of those votes at the end of time does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(m,l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Happy Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.6.3, pp. 54–55.
property Happy Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,l,v))

Cascade Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant. The source learner must also be safe at every participant at the end of time.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.5.5, pp. 53–54.
property Cascade Termination [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,v. ((♢[a,b] ⊤) ∧ (□[b] live) ∧ (□[] safe(l))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v) ⇒ live ⇒
  ↕ deliver(b,l,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.4.1, p. 52.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[a,b] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

Paper and interpretation

Implementation authorship: this executable theory was AI-generated following prompts by Murdoch J. Gabbay. Automated validation is described in the package; no independent expert audit of this translation is claimed. Source-paper authorship is listed separately.

Paper draft: Heterogeneous trust in reliable broadcast via modal logic and history structures, Murdoch J. Gabbay and Isaac Sheff, 2026-11-18. References use the draft's printed page numbers.

Paper basis: HBBSafe, Definition 6.2.2, p. 47; Figure 8, p. 48. Correctness: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49. Proofs: Happy Termination: Proposition 6.6.3, pp. 54–55; Cascade Termination: Proposition 6.5.5, pp. 53–54; Agreement: Proposition 6.4.1, p. 52.

Pedagogical completed-run scenario: the protocol axioms and conditional correctness formulas in this document are unmodified translations of the paper. The singleton history, positive facts and final observation are supplied for this example; they are not a literal paper theory or a proof over all histories.

Code event order: propose(v), echo(v), vote(l,v), and deliver(m,l,v): m is the reporting learner, l the source learner, and v the value (Notation 6.2.3 and Remark 6.2.4, p. 47). HBBCorr instead uses the pair deliver(l,v). Learners and values share one domain (Definition 3.1.1, p. 21).

include ThyLive keeps Figure 7, p. 43, Definition 5.2.4 dynamic: LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both complete Knowledge schemes, over all ground events, with a single learner in each Knowledge□ instance, are checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 42). The schemes regenerate when the history changes. Full source and notation map; paper variants and their status.

HBBSafe: remove Echo!

A live participant knows the unique proposal and never echoes. The curated browser preset omits Echo!, admitting a model in which Happy Termination fails with its complete premise and trigger true. Cascade Termination and Agreement hold vacuously because there are no deliveries. Restoring Echo! makes the full theory incompatible with this fixed history, so all three claims are then Not tested. Both runs use exactly the same history and facts. Final silent observations preserve the complete Knowledge schemes.

Browser preset: only Echo! is omitted. Keep all axioms selects the full-theory comparison; Use example defaults restores the omission. Neither action starts a run. The source declares every rule: plain Markdown imports and CLI runs retain them unless you specify --drop "Echo!".

HBBSafe: remove Vote!

A live participant knows the unique proposal, echoes it, and never votes. Safety is pinned true at all times, exercising the distinctive persistent-safety premise of HBBSafe Vote!. The curated browser preset omits Vote!, admitting a model in which Happy Termination fails with its complete premise and trigger true. Cascade Termination and Agreement have absent scenarios. Restoring Vote! makes the full theory incompatible with this fixed history, leaving the claims Not tested. Final silent observations preserve the complete Knowledge schemes.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 43, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 42).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires both current safe(l) and knowledge of a quorum of prior matching echoes.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ (safe(l) ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a reporting quorum of matching source-learner votes.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. deliver(m,l,v) ⇒ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

Safe — other assumption

Safety is a biconditional: at most one proposal value is known, or every learner has a sequential witness in every relevant quorum intersection.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2; Remark 6.3.2, pp. 50–51.
axiom Safe [other]:
  ∀ l. safe(l) ⇔ ((∃⩽1 v. ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ∨ (∀ m. ♢[l,m] seq))

Echo! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a proposal, that participant must echo some value at an actual local tuple. The value is existentially chosen; end-of-time knowledge alone does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of echoes, that participant must vote at an actual local tuple. The rule does not impose a time order between those two tuples. Its separate ⇕ safe(l) guard requires safety at every actual local tuple; the required vote is for the same value.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ⇕ safe(l) ⇒ ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ↕ vote(l,v)

Deliver! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of votes, that participant must deliver at an actual local tuple. Merely learning of those votes at the end of time does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(m,l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Happy Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.6.3, pp. 54–55.
property Happy Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,l,v))

Cascade Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant. The source learner must also be safe at every participant at the end of time.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.5.5, pp. 53–54.
property Cascade Termination [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,v. ((♢[a,b] ⊤) ∧ (□[b] live) ∧ (□[] safe(l))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v) ⇒ live ⇒
  ↕ deliver(b,l,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.4.1, p. 52.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[a,b] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

HBBSafe: remove the Safe definition

A live singleton proposes and echoes the unique value, then stops before voting. Safety has no supplied positive facts. In the given interpretation safe(v) is false, so only Safe fails: Vote! is disabled by its persistent-safety premise. With Safe retained, its at-most-one-proposal disjunct forces safe(v) everywhere, enabling Vote! and making this stopped history inconsistent. Omitting only Safe permits safe(v) to remain false and gives a nonvacuous Happy Termination counterexample. The other two correctness scenarios are absent.

This is a genuine HBBSafe definition-removal experiment, not one of the paper's stated incorrect-axiom variants. It uses Remark 6.3.2, pp. 50–51, and Lemma 6.6.2, p. 54: at most one proposed value implies safety. The paired full and omitted rows change only the retained rule selection; the correctness property itself is unchanged.

HBBSafe: a live participant chooses one echo value

The live sequential singleton observes proposals a and b, chooses only echo(a), votes a for both learners and completes all reporting/source deliveries of a. The correct existential Echo! accepts this model; all three complete correctness conditionals hold. Happy Termination has an absent scenario because its unique-proposal premise is false. Cascade Termination and Agreement have present scenarios. Sequential quorum intersections make Safe true even with multiple proposals.

The extra Bad Echo! property is a diagnostic probe of the universally closed incorrect axiom in Remark 6.3.3(2), p. 51: ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ↕ echo(w) for all v,w. It fails at a live world with known proposal a and w=b because echo(b) never occurs. It is not a failed correctness theorem. The paired incorrect-axiom example replaces only Echo! with that formula and has no model. Requiring all values to be echoed overconstrains the choice and conflicts here with EchoNE.

Read the rules below, choose Continue to claims, review the selected properties and assumptions, then continue to the run settings and run the check. Use Edit Markdown to change a rule; Unicode and ASCII spellings have identical semantics. The supplied history JSON is at the end.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 43, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 42).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires both current safe(l) and knowledge of a quorum of prior matching echoes.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ (safe(l) ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a reporting quorum of matching source-learner votes.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. deliver(m,l,v) ⇒ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

Safe — other assumption

Safety is a biconditional: at most one proposal value is known, or every learner has a sequential witness in every relevant quorum intersection.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2; Remark 6.3.2, pp. 50–51.
axiom Safe [other]:
  ∀ l. safe(l) ⇔ ((∃⩽1 v. ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ∨ (∀ m. ♢[l,m] seq))

Echo! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a proposal, that participant must echo some value at an actual local tuple. The value is existentially chosen; end-of-time knowledge alone does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of echoes, that participant must vote at an actual local tuple. The rule does not impose a time order between those two tuples. Its separate ⇕ safe(l) guard requires safety at every actual local tuple; the required vote is for the same value.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ⇕ safe(l) ⇒ ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ↕ vote(l,v)

Deliver! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of votes, that participant must deliver at an actual local tuple. Merely learning of those votes at the end of time does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(m,l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Happy Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.6.3, pp. 54–55.
property Happy Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,l,v))

Cascade Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant. The source learner must also be safe at every participant at the end of time.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.5.5, pp. 53–54.
property Cascade Termination [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,v. ((♢[a,b] ⊤) ∧ (□[b] live) ∧ (□[] safe(l))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v) ⇒ live ⇒
  ↕ deliver(b,l,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.4.1, p. 52.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[a,b] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

Bad Echo! — diagnostic probe

This diagnostic tests the explicitly incorrect universally closed Echo! from Remark 6.3.3(2), p. 51. A failure refutes that candidate axiom, rather than a correctness theorem.

# Scenario: added for this experiment; not a paper axiom or correctness claim. Remark 6.3.3(2), p. 51.
property Bad Echo! [all]:
  ∀ v,w. ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ↕ echo(w)

HBBSafe: the incorrect universal Echo! overconstrains choice

This example has exactly the history, facts, quorums and correctness properties of the valid one-echo choice model. It changes only Echo!, replacing its existentially chosen conclusion by the incorrect formula printed in Remark 6.3.3(2), p. 51, with both free variables universally closed.

The live participant knows proposals a and b but echoes only a. The bad axiom demands eventual echo(b) as well; this fixed history has no model. All three correctness claims are Not tested after that consistency failure. This is an overconstraint demonstration, not a correctness counterexample. In an extension that echoes both distinct values at the singleton, EchoNE would also forbid that choice. The valid example separately probes this precise bad formula and supplies a replayable counterexample to the probe.

HBBSafe: end-of-time knowledge is not actionable

This example isolates the outer ↕ in the forward rules. Participant q proposes v and is nonlive. Participant p is live but has no actual local tuples. At the end of time p knows that v was proposed; p never learns this at a recorded local tuple.

The correct Echo! requires ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) before it requires an echo. Its antecedent is false here, so the full HBBSafe theory permits the supplied model. The extra Bad end-only Echo! property tests the explicitly incorrect formula from Remark 6.3.3(3), p. 51, which lacks that outer ↕. It fails at p’s end-of-time world.

Run the example defaults to see the diagnostic counterexample alongside all three canonical claims. The canonical claims hold with their scenarios absent: no live participant actually learns a proposal, and no delivery occurs. A live participant need not be active; Figure 7 does not assume the optional LiveActive axiom discussed on p. 46. The paired incorrect-axiom example replaces only Echo! and has no model on this same history.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 43, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 42).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires both current safe(l) and knowledge of a quorum of prior matching echoes.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ (safe(l) ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a reporting quorum of matching source-learner votes.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. deliver(m,l,v) ⇒ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

Safe — other assumption

Safety is a biconditional: at most one proposal value is known, or every learner has a sequential witness in every relevant quorum intersection.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Safe [other]:
  ∀ l. safe(l) ⇔ ((∃⩽1 v. ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ∨ (∀ m. ♢[l,m] seq))

Echo! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a proposal, that participant must echo some value at an actual local tuple. The value is existentially chosen; end-of-time knowledge alone does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of echoes, that participant must vote at an actual local tuple. The rule does not impose a time order between those two tuples. Its separate ⇕ safe(l) guard requires safety at every actual local tuple; the required vote is for the same value.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ⇕ safe(l) ⇒ ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ↕ vote(l,v)

Deliver! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of votes, that participant must deliver at an actual local tuple. Merely learning of those votes at the end of time does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(m,l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Happy Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.6.3, pp. 54–55.
property Happy Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,l,v))

Cascade Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant. The source learner must also be safe at every participant at the end of time.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.5.5, pp. 53–54.
property Cascade Termination [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,v. ((♢[a,b] ⊤) ∧ (□[b] live) ∧ (□[] safe(l))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v) ⇒ live ⇒
  ↕ deliver(b,l,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.4.1, p. 52.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[a,b] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

Bad end-only Echo! — diagnostic probe

The candidate omits the antecedent’s outer ↕. At participant p’s end-of-time world, live and the known proposal are true, but no actual p tuple records an echo. A failure here refutes this candidate axiom; it does not refute a protocol correctness claim.

# Scenario: diagnostic of the explicitly incorrect axiom in Remark 6.3.3(3), p. 51; not a paper correctness claim.
property Bad end-only Echo! [all]:
  ∀ v. (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

This example has exactly the participants, history, facts, quorums and correctness formulas of the valid end-only-knowledge model. It changes only Echo!, replacing the paper’s actual-local antecedent by the explicitly incorrect formula in Remark 6.3.3(3), p. 51.

HBBSafe: full Vote? rejects unsafe votes

Source learners a and b have disjoint singleton quorums {q} and {r}; reporting learner c has the sequential singleton quorum {p}. Participant q echoes a and r echoes b without local equivocation. Participant p votes for the two different source learners and delivers both values via reporter c. The exact Safe definition is retained; positive facts record its true instances at the declared prefixes. After both proposals, the disjoint intersections make these learners unsafe. A scenario-only NoLive axiom keeps all participants non-live, so the forward obligations are vacuous. The example therefore isolates safety from liveness.

This full-guard control has no model: the correct Vote? requires safe(l), which is false at the offending votes. All three correctness claims are therefore Not tested.

The omitted-guard companion deletes only that conjunct, leaving quorum support, EchoNE, Safe and all ThyLive schemes intact. That edited theory admits a nonvacuous Agreement counterexample on the same history. In that counterexample, both reporting variables of Agreement are assigned learner c, its source variables l and m are assigned learners a and b, and the delivered values are the distinct a and b. HBBSafe Agreement constrains reporting intersections; the distinct source quorums need not intersect. Both liveness scenarios are absent. This deliberate local weakening is not claimed to be one of the paper's incorrect examples; its relevance follows from Figure 8 and the Agreement proof, Proposition 6.4.1, p. 52.

  ∀ m,l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(m,l,v)

NoLive — other assumption

This scenario assumption makes every participant non-live at every possible world. It isolates the safety question from liveness obligations.

# Scenario: added for this experiment; not a paper axiom or correctness claim.
axiom NoLive [other]:
  ¬ live

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Happy Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.6.3, pp. 54–55.
property Happy Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,l,v))

Cascade Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant. The source learner must also be safe at every participant at the end of time.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.5.5, pp. 53–54.
property Cascade Termination [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,v. ((♢[a,b] ⊤) ∧ (□[b] live) ∧ (□[] safe(l))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v) ⇒ live ⇒
  ↕ deliver(b,l,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.4.1, p. 52.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[a,b] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

HBBSafe: omit only the safety guard from Vote?

Source learners a and b have disjoint singleton quorums {q} and {r}; reporting learner c has the sequential singleton quorum {p}. Participant q echoes a and r echoes b without local equivocation. Participant p votes for the two different source learners and delivers both values via reporter c. The exact Safe definition is retained; positive facts record its true instances at the declared prefixes. After both proposals, the disjoint intersections make these learners unsafe. A scenario-only NoLive axiom keeps all participants non-live, so the forward obligations are vacuous. The example therefore isolates safety from liveness.

This edited theory has an Agreement counterexample: it deletes only the safe(l) conjunct from Vote?, leaving quorum support, EchoNE, Safe and all ThyLive schemes intact. The full-guard control on the same history has no model because that conjunct is false at the offending votes.

In that counterexample, both reporting variables of Agreement are assigned learner c, its source variables l and m are assigned learners a and b, and the delivered values are the distinct a and b. HBBSafe Agreement constrains reporting intersections; the distinct source quorums need not intersect. Both liveness scenarios are absent. This deliberate local weakening is not claimed to be one of the paper's incorrect examples; its relevance follows from Figure 8 and the Agreement proof, Proposition 6.4.1, p. 52.

Read the rules below, choose Continue to claims, review the selected properties and assumptions, then continue to the run settings and run the check. Use Edit Markdown to change a rule; Unicode and ASCII spellings have identical semantics. The supplied history JSON is at the end.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 43, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 42).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

This experimental weakening removes only the safe(l) guard. Knowledge of a quorum of prior matching echoes is still required.

# Scenario: added for this experiment; not a paper axiom or correctness claim. Figure 8.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ □[l] ↓ echo(v)

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a reporting quorum of matching source-learner votes.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. deliver(m,l,v) ⇒ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

Safe — other assumption

Safety is a biconditional: at most one proposal value is known, or every learner has a sequential witness in every relevant quorum intersection.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2; Remark 6.3.2, pp. 50–51.
axiom Safe [other]:
  ∀ l. safe(l) ⇔ ((∃⩽1 v. ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ∨ (∀ m. ♢[l,m] seq))

Echo! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a proposal, that participant must echo some value at an actual local tuple. The value is existentially chosen; end-of-time knowledge alone does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of echoes, that participant must vote at an actual local tuple. The rule does not impose a time order between those two tuples. Its separate ⇕ safe(l) guard requires safety at every actual local tuple; the required vote is for the same value.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ⇕ safe(l) ⇒ ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ↕ vote(l,v)

Deliver! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of votes, that participant must deliver at an actual local tuple. Merely learning of those votes at the end of time does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 48; Definition 6.2.2.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(m,l,v)

NoLive — other assumption

This scenario assumption makes every participant non-live at every possible world. It isolates the safety question from liveness obligations.

# Scenario: added for this experiment; not a paper axiom or correctness claim.
axiom NoLive [other]:
  ¬ live

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Happy Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.6.3, pp. 54–55.
property Happy Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,l,v))

Cascade Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant. The source learner must also be safe at every participant at the end of time.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.5.5, pp. 53–54.
property Cascade Termination [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,v. ((♢[a,b] ⊤) ∧ (□[b] live) ∧ (□[] safe(l))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v) ⇒ live ⇒
  ↕ deliver(b,l,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 48; Theorem 6.2.6, p. 49; Proposition 6.4.1, p. 52.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[a,b] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

HBBSimp — completed broadcast

This is a completed one-participant run of HBBSimp, using the axioms and correctness statements from the draft of 18 November 2026. Choose Use this history; find facts first. The given positive facts pin liveness; the retained axioms constrain the remaining predicate interpretation.

The final silent † tuple records knowledge of delivery. It is not an extra protocol event. Removing that observation can violate the Knowledge scheme, even though delivery itself has occurred.

The correctness formulas include their stated premises. A true implication may be vacuous. For a direct non-vacuity investigation, the API supplies the corresponding scenario formulas through correctnessProperties("HBBSimp"). In this completed singleton example all three scenarios occur.

Read the rules below, choose Continue to claims, review the selected properties and assumptions, then continue to the run settings and run the check. Use Edit Markdown to change a rule; Unicode and ASCII spellings have identical semantics. The supplied history JSON is at the end.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 43, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 42).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires knowledge of a source quorum of prior matching echoes.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ □[l] ↓ echo(v)

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a reporting quorum of matching source-learner votes.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. deliver(m,l,v) ⇒ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

Echo! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a proposal, that participant must echo some value at an actual local tuple. The value is existentially chosen; end-of-time knowledge alone does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of echoes, that participant must vote at an actual local tuple. The rule does not impose a time order between those two tuples. The required vote is for the same value.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ↕ vote(l,v)

Deliver! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of votes, that participant must deliver at an actual local tuple. Merely learning of those votes at the end of time does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(m,l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Happy Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 57; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 57; Proposition 7.3.3, pp. 59–60.
property Happy Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,l,v))

Cascade Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 57; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 57; Proposition 7.3.2, pp. 59–60.
property Cascade Termination [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,v. ((♢[a,b] ⊤) ∧ (□[b] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(b,l,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 57; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 57; Proposition 7.3.1, p. 59.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[l,m] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

Paper and interpretation

Implementation authorship: this executable theory was AI-generated following prompts by Murdoch J. Gabbay. Automated validation is described in the package; no independent expert audit of this translation is claimed. Source-paper authorship is listed separately.

Paper draft: Heterogeneous trust in reliable broadcast via modal logic and history structures, Murdoch J. Gabbay and Isaac Sheff, 2026-11-18. References use the draft's printed page numbers.

Paper basis: HBBSimp, Definition 7.1.1, p. 56; Figure 10, p. 57. Correctness: Figure 11, p. 57; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 57. Proofs: Happy Termination: Proposition 7.3.3, pp. 59–60; Cascade Termination: Proposition 7.3.2, pp. 59–60; Agreement: Proposition 7.3.1, p. 59.

Pedagogical completed-run scenario: the protocol axioms and conditional correctness formulas in this document are unmodified translations of the paper. The singleton history, positive facts and final observation are supplied for this example; they are not a literal paper theory or a proof over all histories.

Code event order: propose(v), echo(v), vote(l,v), and deliver(m,l,v): m is the reporting learner, l the source learner, and v the value (Notation 6.2.3 and Remark 6.2.4, p. 47). HBBCorr instead uses the pair deliver(l,v). Learners and values share one domain (Definition 3.1.1, p. 21).

include ThyLive keeps Figure 7, p. 43, Definition 5.2.4 dynamic: LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both complete Knowledge schemes, over all ground events, with a single learner in each Knowledge□ instance, are checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 42). The schemes regenerate when the history changes. Full source and notation map; paper variants and their status.

What EchoNE rules out

This deliberately unsuitable history is a single sequential chain: red and blue are proposed, both are echoed, and both are voted for and delivered. NoLive makes the participant non-live; it remains sequential.

The curated browser preset omits EchoNE. Run Use this history; find facts to find a model in which Agreement is false: its sequential quorum-intersection premise holds, but the two delivered values differ.

Choose Keep all axioms for the comparison. EchoNE then rejects the real conflicting echoes, and changing predicate truth values cannot repair this fixed history. The result is no model, with all correctness claims Not tested; it is not an Agreement proof. In the omission run, both liveness claims hold with absent scenarios: NoLive excludes their live-quorum premise, and two distinct values are proposed. The saved evidence records the omission and can be replayed. All three full correctness formulas are checked by node demo.mjs.

Browser preset: only EchoNE is omitted. Keep all axioms selects the full-theory comparison; Use example defaults restores the omission. Neither action starts a run. The source declares every rule: plain Markdown imports and CLI runs retain them unless you specify --drop "EchoNE".

When EchoNE constrains only live participants

This uses exactly the sequential two-value history and NoLive assumption from echo-ne.md. Every declared axiom is retained, including the complete dynamic ThyLive include. The only edit to the protocol is EchoNE: its prohibition now applies only when the participant is live.

Use this history; find facts finds a model of all the edited assumptions, yet Agreement fails with a sequential quorum intersection and two conflicting deliveries. NoLive makes the weakened EchoNE true without excluding those echoes; ThyLive permits a non-live participant to be sequential. Happy Termination and Cascade Termination hold with absent scenarios.

The unedited EchoNE on this same history gives no model, which is not a proof of Agreement. This concrete countermodel shows that the live-only restriction loses this Agreement guarantee for the selected finite scope. It makes no unbounded claim about all weakenings. Run node demo.mjs for the full comparison and independently replayed evidence.

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 57; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 57; Proposition 7.3.1, p. 59.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[l,m] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires knowledge of a source quorum of prior matching echoes.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ □[l] ↓ echo(v)

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a reporting quorum of matching source-learner votes.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. deliver(m,l,v) ⇒ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

Echo! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a proposal, that participant must echo some value at an actual local tuple. The value is existentially chosen; end-of-time knowledge alone does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of echoes, that participant must vote at an actual local tuple. The rule does not impose a time order between those two tuples. The required vote is for the same value.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ↕ vote(l,v)

Deliver! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of votes, that participant must deliver at an actual local tuple. Merely learning of those votes at the end of time does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(m,l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Happy Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 57; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 57; Proposition 7.3.3, pp. 59–60.
property Happy Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,l,v))

Cascade Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 57; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 57; Proposition 7.3.2, pp. 59–60.
property Cascade Termination [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,v. ((♢[a,b] ⊤) ∧ (□[b] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(b,l,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 57; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 57; Proposition 7.3.1, p. 59.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[l,m] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 43, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 42).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires knowledge of a source quorum of prior matching echoes.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ □[l] ↓ echo(v)

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a reporting quorum of matching source-learner votes.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. deliver(m,l,v) ⇒ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

Echo! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a proposal, that participant must echo some value at an actual local tuple. The value is existentially chosen; end-of-time knowledge alone does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of echoes, that participant must vote at an actual local tuple. The rule does not impose a time order between those two tuples. The required vote is for the same value.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ↕ vote(l,v)

Deliver! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of votes, that participant must deliver at an actual local tuple. Merely learning of those votes at the end of time does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 57; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(m,l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Happy Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 57; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 57; Proposition 7.3.3, pp. 59–60.
property Happy Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,l,v))

Cascade Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 57; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 57; Proposition 7.3.2, pp. 59–60.
property Cascade Termination [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,v. ((♢[a,b] ⊤) ∧ (□[b] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(b,l,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 57; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 57; Proposition 7.3.1, p. 59.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[l,m] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

HBBCorr — completed broadcast

This is a completed one-participant run of HBBCorr, using the axioms and correctness statements from the draft of 18 November 2026. Choose Use this history; find facts first. The given positive facts pin liveness and correlation; the retained axioms constrain the remaining predicate interpretation.

The final silent † tuple records knowledge of delivery. It is not an extra protocol event. Removing that observation can violate the Knowledge scheme, even though delivery itself has occurred.

The correctness formulas include their stated premises. A true implication may be vacuous. For a direct non-vacuity investigation, the API supplies the corresponding scenario formulas through correctnessProperties("HBBCorr"). In this completed singleton example all three scenarios occur.

Read the rules below, choose Continue to claims, review the selected properties and assumptions, then continue to the run settings and run the check. Use Edit Markdown to change a rule; Unicode and ASCII spellings have identical semantics. The supplied history JSON is at the end.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 43, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 42).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires either quorum echoes of that value, or knowledge of a matching vote for a currently correlated learner.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ ((□[l] ↓ echo(v)) ∨ (∃ m. (corr(m,l) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v))))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a quorum of matching votes for the same learner.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. deliver(l,v) ⇒ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

VoteNE — other assumption

An actual local vote and an earlier local vote for correlated learners must carry the same value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom VoteNE [other]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. vote(l,v) ⇒ ↓ vote(m,w) ⇒ corr(l,m) ⇒ v=w

3twined — other assumption

Every triple of independently chosen learner quorums must have a common participant. Repeated learner names still make independent quorum choices.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom 3twined [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. ♢[l,m,n] ⊤

CorrSeq — other assumption

For every choice of one quorum from each correlated learner, their intersection must contain a sequential participant.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom CorrSeq [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ♢[l,m] seq

CorrPast — other assumption

Correlation persists to every actual earlier local tuple. Its temporal operator ranges over recorded local tuples, rather than every hypothetical world.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom CorrPast [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ⇓ corr(l,m)

CorrSymm — other assumption

Correlation is symmetric. Reflexivity is not an additional assumption.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom CorrSymm [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,l)

CorrTran — other assumption

Correlation is transitive.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom CorrTran [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,n) ⇒ corr(l,n)

Echo! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a proposal, that participant must echo some value at an actual local tuple. The value is existentially chosen; end-of-time knowledge alone does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of echoes, that participant must vote at an actual local tuple. The rule does not impose a time order between those two tuples. The vote value remains existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Vote'! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a correlated source vote, and correlation holds at every actual local tuple, that participant must vote for some value at an actual local tuple. The existential value choice is retained.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom Vote'! [forward]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ↕ (live ∧ ⇕ corr(l,m) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Deliver! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of votes, that participant must deliver at an actual local tuple. Merely learning of those votes at the end of time does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Happy Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.5.1, p. 66.
property Happy Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v))

Cascade Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.4.5, pp. 65–66.
property Cascade Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ((□[] corr(l,m)) ∧ (□[m] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(m,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.3.1, p. 64.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. ((□[] corr(l,m))) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(m,w)) ⇒ v=w)

Paper and interpretation

The paper writes correlation as l ≐ m. In Figure 12, p. 63, CorrSeq, CorrPast, CorrSymm and CorrTran denote ≐seq, ≐⇓, ≐symm and ≐tran. The executable predicate is corr(l,m). Correlation is distinct from value equality; both voting forward rules retain the paper’s existential value choice.

A live proposal stops before echoing

This is a pedagogical Echo! omission. The complete protocol chain would be proposal → echo → vote → delivery. This supplied history has one live sequential participant and stops after the proposal. The final silent † tuple observes the latest real event and supplies the eventual knowledge required by ThyLive; it is not an additional protocol action.

Echo! is the sole failed original rule. Removing it leaves a known unique proposal but no echo, vote, or delivery, so Happy Termination fails with its premise and trigger true. Cascade Termination and Agreement have absent scenarios. The progress rules are Figure 12; compare Happy Termination’s proof in Proposition 8.5.1, p. 66.

Browser preset: only Echo! is omitted. Keep all axioms selects the full-theory comparison; Use example defaults restores the omission. Neither action starts a run. The source declares every rule: plain Markdown imports and CLI runs retain them unless you specify --drop "Echo!".

axiom CorrSymm [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,l)

CorrTran — other assumption

Correlation is transitive.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrTran [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,n) ⇒ corr(l,n)

Echo! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a proposal, that participant must echo some value at an actual local tuple. The value is existentially chosen; end-of-time knowledge alone does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of echoes, that participant must vote at an actual local tuple. The rule does not impose a time order between those two tuples. The vote value remains existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Vote'! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a correlated source vote, and correlation holds at every actual local tuple, that participant must vote for some value at an actual local tuple. The existential value choice is retained.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote'! [forward]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ↕ (live ∧ ⇕ corr(l,m) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Deliver! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of votes, that participant must deliver at an actual local tuple. Merely learning of those votes at the end of time does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Happy Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.5.1, p. 66.
property Happy Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v))

Cascade Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.4.5, pp. 65–66.
property Cascade Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ((□[] corr(l,m)) ∧ (□[m] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(m,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.3.1, p. 64.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. ((□[] corr(l,m))) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(m,w)) ⇒ v=w)

A live echo stops before voting

This is a pedagogical Vote! omission. The complete protocol chain would be proposal → echo → vote → delivery. This supplied history has one live sequential participant and stops after the echo. The final silent † tuple observes the latest real event and supplies the eventual knowledge required by ThyLive; it is not an additional protocol action.

Vote! is the sole failed original rule. Removing it leaves a quorum echo of the known unique value but no vote or delivery, so Happy Termination fails nonvacuously. Vote'! remains selected: it has no source vote from which to propagate, so it does not repair this prefix. Cascade Termination and Agreement have absent scenarios. The progress rules are Figure 12; compare Happy Termination’s proof in Proposition 8.5.1, p. 66.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires either quorum echoes of that value, or knowledge of a matching vote for a currently correlated learner.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ ((□[l] ↓ echo(v)) ∨ (∃ m. (corr(m,l) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v))))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a quorum of matching votes for the same learner.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. deliver(l,v) ⇒ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

VoteNE — other assumption

An actual local vote and an earlier local vote for correlated learners must carry the same value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom VoteNE [other]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. vote(l,v) ⇒ ↓ vote(m,w) ⇒ corr(l,m) ⇒ v=w

3twined — other assumption

Every triple of independently chosen learner quorums must have a common participant. Repeated learner names still make independent quorum choices.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom 3twined [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. ♢[l,m,n] ⊤

CorrSeq — other assumption

For every choice of one quorum from each correlated learner, their intersection must contain a sequential participant.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrSeq [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ♢[l,m] seq

CorrPast — other assumption

Correlation persists to every actual earlier local tuple. Its temporal operator ranges over recorded local tuples, rather than every hypothetical world.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrPast [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ⇓ corr(l,m)

CorrSymm — other assumption

Correlation is symmetric. Reflexivity is not an additional assumption.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrSymm [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,l)

  ∀ l,m,n. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,n) ⇒ corr(l,n)

Happy Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.5.1, p. 66.
property Happy Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v))

Cascade Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.4.5, pp. 65–66.
property Cascade Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ((□[] corr(l,m)) ∧ (□[m] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(m,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.3.1, p. 64.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. ((□[] corr(l,m))) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(m,w)) ⇒ v=w)

Correlation propagation without Vote'!

This is a pedagogical Vote'! omission, specifically exercising Cascade Termination. The two live participants propose different values and each echoes only its own value. Learner a has quorum {p}; learner b has quorum {p,q}. Both participants vote for and deliver a’s value, with final silent observations ensuring the complete Knowledge schemes hold. Every learner is correlated everywhere, and all local histories are sequential. The mixed echo quorum {p,q} never unanimously supports any value, so Vote! cannot initiate a b-vote.

The source a-vote activates Vote'!, which is the sole failed original rule. Omitting it prevents any b-delivery, so Cascade Termination fails with correlation, a live b-quorum, and source delivery all present. Happy Termination’s unique-proposal scenario is absent; Agreement holds with a delivery scenario present. The rule’s role is discussed in Proposition 8.4.5, pp. 65–66, and footnote 64, p. 62: the paper’s ⇕ corr premise is deliberate.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 43, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 42).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires either quorum echoes of that value, or knowledge of a matching vote for a currently correlated learner.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ ((□[l] ↓ echo(v)) ∨ (∃ m. (corr(m,l) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v))))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a quorum of matching votes for the same learner.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. deliver(l,v) ⇒ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

VoteNE — other assumption

An actual local vote and an earlier local vote for correlated learners must carry the same value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom VoteNE [other]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. vote(l,v) ⇒ ↓ vote(m,w) ⇒ corr(l,m) ⇒ v=w

3twined — other assumption

Every triple of independently chosen learner quorums must have a common participant. Repeated learner names still make independent quorum choices.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom 3twined [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. ♢[l,m,n] ⊤

CorrSeq — other assumption

For every choice of one quorum from each correlated learner, their intersection must contain a sequential participant.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrSeq [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ♢[l,m] seq

CorrPast — other assumption

Correlation persists to every actual earlier local tuple. Its temporal operator ranges over recorded local tuples, rather than every hypothetical world.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrPast [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ⇓ corr(l,m)

CorrSymm — other assumption

Correlation is symmetric. Reflexivity is not an additional assumption.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrSymm [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,l)

CorrTran — other assumption

Correlation is transitive.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrTran [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,n) ⇒ corr(l,n)

Echo! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a proposal, that participant must echo some value at an actual local tuple. The value is existentially chosen; end-of-time knowledge alone does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of echoes, that participant must vote at an actual local tuple. The rule does not impose a time order between those two tuples. The vote value remains existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Vote'! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a correlated source vote, and correlation holds at every actual local tuple, that participant must vote for some value at an actual local tuple. The existential value choice is retained.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote'! [forward]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ↕ (live ∧ ⇕ corr(l,m) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Deliver! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of votes, that participant must deliver at an actual local tuple. Merely learning of those votes at the end of time does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v)

  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒

A correlated fork without CorrSeq

This is a pedagogical CorrSeq omission, not the literal full theory. One participant has two incomparable causal branches, each with its own proposal, echo, vote, and delivery. Both values use the singleton quorum. Each branch satisfies the backward rules; because neither branch contains the other, EchoNE and VoteNE see no earlier conflicting event. Correlation is pinned everywhere. At the end that participant is not sequential, so CorrSeq alone rejects the history. Omitting CorrSeq admits both different deliveries: Agreement fails with its correlation premise and delivery trigger present. Both liveness scenarios are absent. The paper explains the role of sequential quorum intersections in Agreement’s proof, Proposition 8.3.1, p. 64.

The added NoLive scenario rule fixes live false. Consequently the forward rules and both Knowledge schemes remain present and hold; these examples exercise safety, not progress. This is an explicit model scenario, not a proposed replacement for a paper axiom.
