  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ♢[l,m] seq

CorrPast — other assumption

Correlation persists to every actual earlier local tuple. Its temporal operator ranges over recorded local tuples, rather than every hypothetical world.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrPast [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ⇓ corr(l,m)

CorrSymm — other assumption

Correlation is symmetric. Reflexivity is not an additional assumption.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrSymm [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,l)

CorrTran — other assumption

Correlation is transitive.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrTran [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,n) ⇒ corr(l,n)

Echo! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a proposal, that participant must echo some value at an actual local tuple. The value is existentially chosen; end-of-time knowledge alone does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of echoes, that participant must vote at an actual local tuple. The rule does not impose a time order between those two tuples. The vote value remains existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Vote'! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a correlated source vote, and correlation holds at every actual local tuple, that participant must vote for some value at an actual local tuple. The existential value choice is retained.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote'! [forward]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ↕ (live ∧ ⇕ corr(l,m) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Deliver! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of votes, that participant must deliver at an actual local tuple. Merely learning of those votes at the end of time does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Happy Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.5.1, p. 66.
property Happy Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v))

Cascade Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.4.5, pp. 65–66.
property Cascade Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ((□[] corr(l,m)) ∧ (□[m] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(m,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.3.1, p. 64.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. ((□[] corr(l,m))) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(m,w)) ⇒ v=w)

Correlation learned too late without CorrPast

This is a pedagogical CorrPast omission. The participant r forks, while s is sequential. A first vote for learner c supports votes for a through a local correlation class {a,c}; a separate echo branch supports b. Learners a and b each have quorum {r,s}, and c has quorum {r}. The sequential member s witnesses CorrSeq for a and b at the end. Only at the end does the supplied interpretation relate a to b at every participant. Because that relation was absent at the sequential conflicting votes, VoteNE does not apply there.

CorrPast is the sole failed original rule; omitting it makes Agreement false with its complete end-of-time premise and both deliveries present. Both liveness scenarios are absent. See the backward persistence used in Proposition 8.3.1, p. 64, and the valid alternate temporal formulation in Remark 8.3.2, p. 64.

The added NoLive scenario rule fixes live false. Consequently the forward rules and both Knowledge schemes remain present and hold; these examples exercise safety, not progress. This is an explicit model scenario, not a proposed replacement for a paper axiom.

Browser preset: only CorrPast is omitted. Keep all axioms selects the full-theory comparison; Use example defaults restores the omission. Neither action starts a run. The source declares every rule: plain Markdown imports and CLI runs retain them unless you specify --drop "CorrPast".

Read the rules below, choose Continue to claims, review the selected properties and assumptions, then continue to the run settings and run the check. Use Edit Markdown to change a rule; Unicode and ASCII spellings have identical semantics. The supplied history JSON is at the end.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 43, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 42).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

NoLive — other assumption

This scenario assumption makes every participant non-live at every possible world. It isolates the safety question from liveness obligations.

# Scenario: added for this experiment; not a paper axiom or correctness claim.
axiom NoLive [other]:
  ¬ live

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires either quorum echoes of that value, or knowledge of a matching vote for a currently correlated learner.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ ((□[l] ↓ echo(v)) ∨ (∃ m. (corr(m,l) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v))))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a quorum of matching votes for the same learner.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. deliver(l,v) ⇒ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

VoteNE — other assumption

An actual local vote and an earlier local vote for correlated learners must carry the same value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom VoteNE [other]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. vote(l,v) ⇒ ↓ vote(m,w) ⇒ corr(l,m) ⇒ v=w

3twined — other assumption

Every triple of independently chosen learner quorums must have a common participant. Repeated learner names still make independent quorum choices.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom 3twined [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. ♢[l,m,n] ⊤

CorrSeq — other assumption

For every choice of one quorum from each correlated learner, their intersection must contain a sequential participant.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrSeq [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ♢[l,m] seq

CorrPast — other assumption

Correlation persists to every actual earlier local tuple. Its temporal operator ranges over recorded local tuples, rather than every hypothetical world.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrPast [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ⇓ corr(l,m)

CorrSymm — other assumption

Correlation is symmetric. Reflexivity is not an additional assumption.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrSymm [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,l)

CorrTran — other assumption

Correlation is transitive.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrTran [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,n) ⇒ corr(l,n)

Sequential correlated votes without VoteNE

This is a pedagogical VoteNE omission. It uses the same quorum pattern as the temporal-correlation example, but pins a and b as correlated throughout the entire history. Early local source correlations with c form a complete class {a,b,c} and are closed over each participant’s local past; later they may disappear. This satisfies CorrPast, CorrSymm, and CorrTran.

The forked r can support distinct echo values on separate branches while s stays sequential. At s, vote(a,a) precedes vote(b,b); their learners correlate, so VoteNE is the sole failed rule. EchoNE remains true because each participant has no sequential pair of conflicting echoes. Removing VoteNE admits both quorum-backed deliveries and falsifies Agreement nonvacuously. The need for vote non-equivocation is visible in the VoteNE rule of Figure 12 and Agreement’s Proposition 8.3.1, p. 64; this is not an EchoNE counterexample.

The added NoLive scenario rule fixes live false. Consequently the forward rules and both Knowledge schemes remain present and hold; these examples exercise safety, not progress. This is an explicit model scenario, not a proposed replacement for a paper axiom.

Browser preset: only VoteNE is omitted. Keep all axioms selects the full-theory comparison; Use example defaults restores the omission. Neither action starts a run. The source declares every rule: plain Markdown imports and CLI runs retain them unless you specify --drop "VoteNE".

Read the rules below, choose Continue to claims, review the selected properties and assumptions, then continue to the run settings and run the check. Use Edit Markdown to change a rule; Unicode and ASCII spellings have identical semantics. The supplied history JSON is at the end.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 43, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 42).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

NoLive — other assumption

This scenario assumption makes every participant non-live at every possible world. It isolates the safety question from liveness obligations.

# Scenario: added for this experiment; not a paper axiom or correctness claim.
axiom NoLive [other]:
  ¬ live

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires either quorum echoes of that value, or knowledge of a matching vote for a currently correlated learner.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ ((□[l] ↓ echo(v)) ∨ (∃ m. (corr(m,l) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v))))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a quorum of matching votes for the same learner.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. deliver(l,v) ⇒ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

VoteNE — other assumption

An actual local vote and an earlier local vote for correlated learners must carry the same value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom VoteNE [other]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. vote(l,v) ⇒ ↓ vote(m,w) ⇒ corr(l,m) ⇒ v=w

3twined — other assumption

Every triple of independently chosen learner quorums must have a common participant. Repeated learner names still make independent quorum choices.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom 3twined [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. ♢[l,m,n] ⊤

CorrSeq — other assumption

For every choice of one quorum from each correlated learner, their intersection must contain a sequential participant.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrSeq [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ♢[l,m] seq

CorrPast — other assumption

Correlation persists to every actual earlier local tuple. Its temporal operator ranges over recorded local tuples, rather than every hypothetical world.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrPast [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ⇓ corr(l,m)

CorrSymm — other assumption

Correlation is symmetric. Reflexivity is not an additional assumption.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrSymm [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,l)

CorrTran — other assumption

Correlation is transitive.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrTran [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,n) ⇒ corr(l,n)

Echo! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a proposal, that participant must echo some value at an actual local tuple. The value is existentially chosen; end-of-time knowledge alone does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of echoes, that participant must vote at an actual local tuple. The rule does not impose a time order between those two tuples. The vote value remains existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Vote'! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a correlated source vote, and correlation holds at every actual local tuple, that participant must vote for some value at an actual local tuple. The existential value choice is retained.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote'! [forward]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ↕ (live ∧ ⇕ corr(l,m) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Deliver! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of votes, that participant must deliver at an actual local tuple. Merely learning of those votes at the end of time does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Happy Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.5.1, p. 66.
property Happy Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v))

Cascade Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.4.5, pp. 65–66.
property Cascade Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ((□[] corr(l,m)) ∧ (□[m] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(m,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.3.1, p. 64.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. ((□[] corr(l,m))) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(m,w)) ⇒ v=w)

Paper and interpretation

Implementation authorship: this executable theory was AI-generated following prompts by Murdoch J. Gabbay. Automated validation is described in the package; no independent expert audit of this translation is claimed. Source-paper authorship is listed separately.

Source: Murdoch J. Gabbay and Isaac Sheff, Heterogeneous trust in reliable broadcast via modal logic and history structures, draft 18 November 2026 (2026-11-18; the supplied hbb-disc draft).

The protocol rules are Figure 12, p. 63, Definition 8.2.1, p. 62. The three conditional claims are Figure 13, p. 63, Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64: Agreement is proved in Proposition 8.3.1, p. 64; Cascade Termination in Proposition 8.4.5, pp. 65–66; Happy Termination in Proposition 8.5.1, p. 66. The executable names CorrSeq, CorrPast, CorrSymm, and CorrTran denote the paper’s dotted-equality rules (≐seq), (≐⇓), (≐symm), and (≐tran). Here vote(l,v) and deliver(l,v) have two arguments: learner first, broadcast value second.

This document is a pedagogical scenario/experiment, not a literal paper theory listing. The matrix applies exactly the omission or replacement described above; every other protocol axiom and the complete dynamic ThyLive include remain selected. A no-model result concerns this exact history and is not a proof of a correctness theorem. Every false conditional is checked with its full premise and trigger true at the recorded failure binding. A true claim with an absent scenario is vacuous here. See the paper map and paper variants for the complete source correspondence. HBBSafe and HBBSimp use three-argument deliveries, whereas this HBBCorr example uses deliver(l,v).

Pairwise overlap cannot replace 3twined

This is a pedagogical 3twined omission. The learner quorums are a={p,r}, b={p,q}, and c={q,r}: every pair overlaps, but the triple intersection is empty.

Participants p and q are live and sequential; non-live r has separate echo branches. The early q-prefix correlates {a,b,c}, so q can relay c’s value b into a- and b-votes before it sees r’s fork. Later p chooses value a for its a- and b-votes. Correlation between a and b persists everywhere; c may be forgotten after those early q-tuples. CorrSeq, CorrPast, CorrSymm, CorrTran, EchoNE, and VoteNE all hold.

Both live participants vote for every learner, satisfying Vote! and Vote'!, and both deliver (a,a) and (c,b). Their b-votes disagree, so the live b-quorum {p,q} never supports a b-delivery. The complete Knowledge schemes hold because both live participants finish with observations of the final history.

Only 3twined fails. Removing it falsifies Cascade Termination for correlated a,b with a live b-quorum and source delivery present. Happy Termination’s unique-proposal scenario is absent, and Agreement holds with a delivery scenario present. Compare the role of triple intersections in Section 8.4, pp. 64–66, and the alternative quorum condition in Remark 8.6.2, p. 67, equation (4). This case shows that pairwise nonempty overlap alone is insufficient.

This larger fixed-history example uses 20 tuples. The curated interface presets 1,000,000 compilation nodes and 60 seconds; the tour uses the corresponding compilation allowance. To run the weakened case directly from the command line:

node src/cli.mjs run examples/theories/hbb3-three-twined.md --drop 3twined --compile-nodes 1000000 --milliseconds 60000

These are resource limits, not changes to the model or correctness claims.

Browser preset: only 3twined is omitted. Keep all axioms selects the full-theory comparison; Use example defaults restores the omission. Neither action starts a run. The source declares every rule: plain Markdown imports and CLI runs retain them unless you specify --drop "3twined".

Read the rules below, choose Continue to claims, review the selected properties and assumptions, then continue to the run settings and run the check. Use Edit Markdown to change a rule; Unicode and ASCII spellings have identical semantics. The supplied history JSON is at the end.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 43, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 42).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires either quorum echoes of that value, or knowledge of a matching vote for a currently correlated learner.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ ((□[l] ↓ echo(v)) ∨ (∃ m. (corr(m,l) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v))))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a quorum of matching votes for the same learner.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. deliver(l,v) ⇒ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

VoteNE — other assumption

An actual local vote and an earlier local vote for correlated learners must carry the same value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom VoteNE [other]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. vote(l,v) ⇒ ↓ vote(m,w) ⇒ corr(l,m) ⇒ v=w

3twined — other assumption

Every triple of independently chosen learner quorums must have a common participant. Repeated learner names still make independent quorum choices.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom 3twined [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. ♢[l,m,n] ⊤

CorrSeq — other assumption

For every choice of one quorum from each correlated learner, their intersection must contain a sequential participant.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrSeq [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ♢[l,m] seq

CorrPast — other assumption

Correlation persists to every actual earlier local tuple. Its temporal operator ranges over recorded local tuples, rather than every hypothetical world.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrPast [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ⇓ corr(l,m)

CorrSymm — other assumption

Correlation is symmetric. Reflexivity is not an additional assumption.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrSymm [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,l)

CorrTran — other assumption

Correlation is transitive.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrTran [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,n) ⇒ corr(l,n)

Echo! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a proposal, that participant must echo some value at an actual local tuple. The value is existentially chosen; end-of-time knowledge alone does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of echoes, that participant must vote at an actual local tuple. The rule does not impose a time order between those two tuples. The vote value remains existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Vote'! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a correlated source vote, and correlation holds at every actual local tuple, that participant must vote for some value at an actual local tuple. The existential value choice is retained.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote'! [forward]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ↕ (live ∧ ⇕ corr(l,m) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Deliver! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of votes, that participant must deliver at an actual local tuple. Merely learning of those votes at the end of time does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Happy Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.5.1, p. 66.
property Happy Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v))

Cascade Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.4.5, pp. 65–66.
property Cascade Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ((□[] corr(l,m)) ∧ (□[m] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(m,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.3.1, p. 64.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. ((□[] corr(l,m))) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(m,w)) ⇒ v=w)

Paper and interpretation

Implementation authorship: this executable theory was AI-generated following prompts by Murdoch J. Gabbay. Automated validation is described in the package; no independent expert audit of this translation is claimed. Source-paper authorship is listed separately.

Source: Murdoch J. Gabbay and Isaac Sheff, Heterogeneous trust in reliable broadcast via modal logic and history structures, draft 18 November 2026 (2026-11-18; the supplied hbb-disc draft).

The protocol rules are Figure 12, p. 63, Definition 8.2.1, p. 62. The three conditional claims are Figure 13, p. 63, Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64: Agreement is proved in Proposition 8.3.1, p. 64; Cascade Termination in Proposition 8.4.5, pp. 65–66; Happy Termination in Proposition 8.5.1, p. 66. The executable names CorrSeq, CorrPast, CorrSymm, and CorrTran denote the paper’s dotted-equality rules (≐seq), (≐⇓), (≐symm), and (≐tran). Here vote(l,v) and deliver(l,v) have two arguments: learner first, broadcast value second.

This document is a pedagogical scenario/experiment, not a literal paper theory listing. Choose Use this history; find facts to search predicate interpretations on the declared DAG, with the supplied positive facts pinned. The matrix applies exactly the omission or replacement described above; every other protocol axiom and the complete dynamic ThyLive include remain selected. A no-model result concerns this exact history and is not a proof of a correctness theorem. Every false conditional is checked with its full premise and trigger true at the recorded failure binding. A true claim with an absent scenario is vacuous here. See the paper map and paper variants for the complete source correspondence. HBBSafe and HBBSimp use three-argument deliveries, whereas this HBBCorr example uses deliver(l,v).

Sequential intersection is not the definition of correlation

This is a full-theory semantic diagnostic, not a weakening counterexample. Learners L, M, N have single quorums {p,a}, {p,a,b}, {p,b}. Every triple intersection contains p, so 3twined holds. The two incomparable silent p-tuples make p nonsequential at the end; a and b remain sequential. Thus ♢[L,M] seq and ♢[M,N] seq hold, but ♢[L,N] seq does not. That pairwise sequential-intersection relation is not transitive.

Empty correlation is nevertheless a valid partial equivalence relation and satisfies every actual HBBCorr rule, including CorrSeq and CorrPast.

All three correctness conditionals hold with absent scenarios. The extra diagnostic property Incorrect correlation equivalence is false. Remarks 8.1.1(2), pp. 54–55, and 8.6.4, p. 61, explain why the stronger biconditional is not an admissible definition: preserving a partial equivalence relation can require dropping a pair even while that pair retains sequential quorum intersections.

The added NoLive scenario rule fixes live false. Consequently the forward rules and both Knowledge schemes remain present and hold; these examples exercise safety, not progress. This is an explicit model scenario, not a proposed replacement for a paper axiom.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 43, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 42).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

NoLive — other assumption

This scenario assumption makes every participant non-live at every possible world. It isolates the safety question from liveness obligations.

# Scenario: added for this experiment; not a paper axiom or correctness claim.
axiom NoLive [other]:
  ¬ live

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires either quorum echoes of that value, or knowledge of a matching vote for a currently correlated learner.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ ((□[l] ↓ echo(v)) ∨ (∃ m. (corr(m,l) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v))))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a quorum of matching votes for the same learner.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. deliver(l,v) ⇒ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

VoteNE — other assumption

An actual local vote and an earlier local vote for correlated learners must carry the same value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom VoteNE [other]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. vote(l,v) ⇒ ↓ vote(m,w) ⇒ corr(l,m) ⇒ v=w

3twined — other assumption

Every triple of independently chosen learner quorums must have a common participant. Repeated learner names still make independent quorum choices.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom 3twined [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. ♢[l,m,n] ⊤

CorrSeq — other assumption

For every choice of one quorum from each correlated learner, their intersection must contain a sequential participant.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrSeq [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ♢[l,m] seq

CorrPast — other assumption

Correlation persists to every actual earlier local tuple. Its temporal operator ranges over recorded local tuples, rather than every hypothetical world.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrPast [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ⇓ corr(l,m)

CorrSymm — other assumption

Correlation is symmetric. Reflexivity is not an additional assumption.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrSymm [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,l)

CorrTran — other assumption

Correlation is transitive.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom CorrTran [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,n) ⇒ corr(l,n)

Echo! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a proposal, that participant must echo some value at an actual local tuple. The value is existentially chosen; end-of-time knowledge alone does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. ↕ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of echoes, that participant must vote at an actual local tuple. The rule does not impose a time order between those two tuples. The vote value remains existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Vote'! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a correlated source vote, and correlation holds at every actual local tuple, that participant must vote for some value at an actual local tuple. The existential value choice is retained.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote'! [forward]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ↕ (live ∧ ⇕ corr(l,m) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Deliver! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of votes, that participant must deliver at an actual local tuple. Merely learning of those votes at the end of time does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Happy Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.5.1, p. 66.
property Happy Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v))

Cascade Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.4.5, pp. 65–66.
property Cascade Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ((□[] corr(l,m)) ∧ (□[m] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(m,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.3.1, p. 64.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. ((□[] corr(l,m))) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(m,w)) ⇒ v=w)

Incorrect correlation equivalence — diagnostic probe

This diagnostic tests the explicitly incorrect equivalence from Remark 8.6.4, p. 68. Its failure is separate from the three protocol correctness claims.

# Scenario: added for this experiment; not a paper axiom or correctness claim. Remark 8.6.4, p. 68.
property Incorrect correlation equivalence [all]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇔ ♢[l,m] seq

Paper and interpretation

Implementation authorship: this executable theory was AI-generated following prompts by Murdoch J. Gabbay. Automated validation is described in the package; no independent expert audit of this translation is claimed. Source-paper authorship is listed separately.

Source: Murdoch J. Gabbay and Isaac Sheff, Heterogeneous trust in reliable broadcast via modal logic and history structures, draft 18 November 2026 (2026-11-18; the supplied hbb-disc draft).

The protocol rules are Figure 12, p. 63, Definition 8.2.1, p. 62. The three conditional claims are Figure 13, p. 63, Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64: Agreement is proved in Proposition 8.3.1, p. 64; Cascade Termination in Proposition 8.4.5, pp. 65–66; Happy Termination in Proposition 8.5.1, p. 66. The executable names CorrSeq, CorrPast, CorrSymm, and CorrTran denote the paper’s dotted-equality rules (≐seq), (≐⇓), (≐symm), and (≐tran). Here vote(l,v) and deliver(l,v) have two arguments: learner first, broadcast value second.

This document is a pedagogical scenario/experiment, not a literal paper theory listing. An incorrect correlation definition overconstrains the DAG

This is the explicitly incorrect replacement from Remark 8.6.4, p. 68. It replaces both CorrSeq and CorrPast by CorrWrong: corr(l,m) ⇔ ♢[l,m] seq; all other Figure 12 rules and full ThyLive stay selected. The declared DAG and quorum basis are identical to the full-theory diagnostic. At the end the equivalence forces corr(L,M) and corr(M,N), but forces corr(L,N) false. Retained CorrTran requires corr(L,N), so no predicate interpretation can satisfy this replacement theory on this fixed DAG.

The full theory admits the same history. This establishes a semantic design failure through overconstraint, not a counterexample to the paper’s correctness theorem. All three canonical claims remain Not tested in the no-model row. The underlying side-choosing issue appears in Remark 8.1.1(2), pp. 60–61.

The added NoLive scenario rule fixes live false. Consequently the forward rules and both Knowledge schemes remain present and hold; these examples exercise safety, not progress. This is an explicit model scenario, not a proposed replacement for a paper axiom.

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing a correlated source vote, and correlation holds at every actual local tuple, that participant must vote for some value at an actual local tuple. The existential value choice is retained.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Vote'! [forward]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ↕ (live ∧ ⇕ corr(l,m) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Deliver! — forward rule

If an actual local tuple records a live participant knowing the required quorum of votes, that participant must deliver at an actual local tuple. Merely learning of those votes at the end of time does not activate the rule.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 63; Definition 8.2.1, p. 62.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ↕ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v)

CorrWrong — other assumption

This deliberately incorrect replacement equates correlation with sequential quorum intersections. Together with retained transitivity, it can reject legitimate history structures.

# Paper: Remark 8.6.4, p. 68. Deliberately incorrect variant.
axiom CorrWrong [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇔ ♢[l,m] seq

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Happy Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.5.1, p. 66.
property Happy Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃=1 w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v))

Cascade Termination — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.4.5, pp. 65–66.
property Cascade Termination [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ((□[] corr(l,m)) ∧ (□[m] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(m,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 13, p. 63; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 64; Proposition 8.3.1, p. 64.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. ((□[] corr(l,m))) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(m,w)) ⇒ v=w)

Repeated learners — pairwise versus triple intersection

Each minimal quorum contains two of the three participants. Every pair of quorums intersects, so this is a valid semifilter and Pairwise intersection holds. Three independently chosen quorums can have empty intersection, so Triple intersection has a counterexample.

Repeating a learner means making another independent quorum choice. It cannot be replaced by one occurrence of that learner. The empty history is sufficient: this distinction concerns the trust structure itself.

Pairwise intersection — property

# Scenario: added for this experiment; not a paper axiom or correctness claim. Lemma 4.1.1(2), pp. 37–38.
property Pairwise intersection [end]:
  ♢["l","l"] ⊤

Triple intersection — property

Every three independently chosen quorums for this learner must intersect. Pairwise intersection alone does not imply this claim.

# Scenario: added for this experiment; not a paper axiom or correctness claim. Lemma 4.1.1(2), pp. 37–38.
property Triple intersection [end]:
  ♢["l","l","l"] ⊤

Heterogeneous learners — individually valid trust

The red and blue learners each have a valid pairwise-intersecting quorum system. Their trust choices differ: a red quorum and a blue quorum can be disjoint.

The first two properties hold on this fixed history/trust structure; Cross-learner intersection is false. The recorded tuples illustrate separate knowledge histories, but no HBB protocol is asserted by this diagnostic. Domain values also serve as learner names, as required by the paper.
